Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] AnyDesk unattended install / password-set and AnyDesk spawning LOLBins (DragonForce delivery) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Potato SeImpersonate privilege-escalation tools (GodPotato/SweetPotato/BadPotato) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — An analysis of incidents at Brazilian educational institutions
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RDP enabled via fDenyTSConnections=0 in LockBit defense-disabling batch script · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Python keylogger executed by a non-developer account (insider, Case 03) · [LLM] LockBit/DragonForce ransom-note fan-out across many directories (mass encryption) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
RDP enabled via fDenyTSConnections=0 in LockBit defense-disabling batch script AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact registry/command action from Case 01's defense-disabling batch script: flipping fDenyTSConnections to 0 (and opening the RDP firewall) to grant attacker remote access after EDR was disabled with stolen admin creds. Article-specific because it anchors on the verbatim reg command excerpt. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim reg command from the article ('fDenyTSConnections /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f') plus the RDP firewall-open follow-on ('netsh ...'), which are high-fidelity because enabling RDP via CLI on an already-managed host is rarely benign. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-builder-leaked-online-by-angry-developer/
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1112 T1562.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin enabling RDP on a new server build via a provisioning script
  • GPO/SCCM/Intune remediation baseline re-asserting fDenyTSConnections
  • Help-desk troubleshooting remote-access issues on a workstation
  • Lab/imaging automation that toggles RDP as part of golden-image prep
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","gpscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Intune","MDM","Provisioning"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and initiating account for the reg/netsh command; confirm whether it ran under a stolen privileged account and whether an EDR-tamper/AV-killer event preceded it on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable/RDP-block the account, and revoke its sessions; verify RDP was not already used inbound (4624 LogonType 10). 3) Hunt: sweep for the same batch script and fDenyTSConnections change across other hosts, and for PsExecSvc.exe / .KEY artifacts and Potato tools indicating lateral movement and privilege escalation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("reg.exe","cmd.exe","netsh.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/d 0","REG_DWORD"))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("advfirewall","Remote Desktop"))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("netsh","firewall","3389"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where (CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections" and CommandLine has_any ("/d 0","REG_DWORD"))
    or (CommandLine has_all ("advfirewall","Remote Desktop"))
    or (CommandLine has_all ("netsh","firewall","3389"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Potato SeImpersonate privilege-escalation tools (GodPotato/SweetPotato/BadPotato) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Potato-family token-abuse tools the article names for privilege escalation in these intrusions. Article-specific: keys on the exact GodPotato/SweetPotato/BadPotato tool names rather than generic token manipulation. Rationale: Uses the three tool names the article explicitly cites for privilege escalation (GodPotato, SweetPotato, BadPotato) plus close variants; these tool names virtually never appear in benign process telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/ • https://ringsafe.in/seimpersonateprivilege-potato-attacks-system/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/unsupported/windows/win_possible_privilege_escalation_using_rotten_potato/
ATT&CKT1134.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagement running Potato PoCs
  • Security researcher malware-analysis sandbox on a corporate host
  • A benign binary coincidentally named with the substring 'potato' (rare; verify hash/signer)
  • Detection-engineering validation using atomic-red-team T1134.001 tests
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\redteam\", @"\pentest\", @"\tools\atomic"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary hash/signer and the parent process; check whether the initiating account holds SeImpersonatePrivilege and what child was spawned as SYSTEM. 2) Contain: isolate the host and suspend the account; capture the binary for analysis before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on SYSTEM-context actions (EDR disable, RDP enable via fDenyTSConnections, PsExecSvc.exe) on the same and neighboring hosts to map the escalation-to-lateral chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(god|sweet|bad|juicy|rogue|rotten|remote|multi|hot|lonely)potato\d*\.exe$"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(god|sweet|bad|juicy|rogue|rotten|remote|multi)potato\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(god|sweet|bad|juicy|rogue|rotten|remote|multi|hot|lonely)potato\d*\.exe$"
    or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(god|sweet|bad|juicy|rogue|rotten|remote|multi)potato\b"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk unattended install / password-set and AnyDesk spawning LOLBins (DragonForce delivery) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts Case 02's use of AnyDesk for remote access and malware delivery: silent/unattended AnyDesk installation, headless password-set, and AnyDesk spawning cmd/powershell/net to stage DragonForce. Article-specific: pivots on AnyDesk as the delivery vector rather than generic RMM abuse. Rationale: Anchors on AnyDesk (the named remote-access tool in Case 02) in two high-signal shapes: unattended-install/password-set flags used by adversaries for silent persistence, and AnyDesk parenting LOLBins used to stage/launch the ransomware. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/
ATT&CKT1219 T1570 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT department mass-deploying AnyDesk via a management script with --install --silent
  • MSP/help-desk configuring unattended access with --set-password
  • AnyDesk auto-update spawning helper processes
  • Legitimate support session where the technician runs cmd/powershell through AnyDesk
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SCCM","Intune","deploy-anydesk") or AccountName in~ ("helpdesk","itsupport"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether AnyDesk is sanctioned on this host and who initiated the install; review the AnyDesk ID/incoming connection and any child process command lines for ransomware staging. 2) Contain: block the AnyDesk relay/connection at the firewall, isolate the host, and suspend the involved account; preserve the AnyDesk logs (connection_trace.txt, ad_svc.trace). 3) Hunt: pivot to other hosts with AnyDesk installed in the same window and check for DragonForce payloads, mass file encryption, and PsExec lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "AnyDesk.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install","--set-password","--silent","--start-with-win","--get-id"))
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AnyDesk.exe" and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","reg.exe","net.exe","net1.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\AnyDesk.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("--install","--set-password","--silent","--start-with-win","--get-id"))
    or (ParentProcessName endswith "\\AnyDesk.exe" and NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","reg.exe","net.exe","net1.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python keylogger executed by a non-developer account (insider, Case 03) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Case 03's insider Python keylogger: a Python interpreter invoking keylogging libraries (pynput/keyboard/pyautogui) or key-capture APIs, run by an account with no prior Python history (anti-join baseline). Article-specific: models the insider angle by pairing the keylogger toolchain with a first-time-Python-for-this-user signal. Rationale: Pairs the keylogger toolchain (pynput/keyboard/pyautogui/GetAsyncKeyState — standard Python input-capture) with a leftanti baseline so it fires when a user with no Python history runs it, matching the article's insider framing in Case 03. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/
ATT&CKT1056.001 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CS student legitimately experimenting with pynput/pyautogui for automation
  • QA/RPA automation using pyautogui for UI testing on a shared lab machine
  • A user installing a game-macro/hotkey tool built in Python
  • Security training/CTF exercise on a sanctioned host
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in~ ("builduser","qa-automation") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\devtools\", @"\ci\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account and its role — does this user normally write code? Locate the .py script (FolderPath/SHA256) and inspect for capture-to-file and exfil logic. 2) Contain: on a shared workstation, suspend the session, capture the script and any output logs (keystroke dumps), and reset credentials for accounts recently used on that host. 3) Hunt: search for the same script hash on other shared machines, for the output/log file being read or emailed, and for the account accessing PII stores (student databases) around the same time.
let Baseline = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
    | summarize by AccountName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pynput","pyautogui","keyboard","keylog","GetAsyncKeyState","SetWindowsHookEx")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountName
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let Baseline = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
    | summarize by SubjectUserName;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("pynput","pyautogui","keyboard","keylog","GetAsyncKeyState","SetWindowsHookEx")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on SubjectUserName
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LockBit/DragonForce ransom-note fan-out across many directories (mass encryption) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact phase of Case 01/02: a single process dropping an identically-named ransom note into many directories as it encrypts local disks and network shares (the leaked-builder config had local_disks and network_shares enabled). Article-specific: models the manual-spread LockBit variant's note fan-out rather than a generic file-write rule. Rationale: Anchors on LockBit's ransom-note drop-in-every-directory behavior (the leaked builder config had local_disks/network_shares true, self_destruct and set_wallpaper), using a distinct-directory fan-out threshold that separates real encryption from a single benign readme.txt. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/incidents-at-brazilian-educational-institutions/120803/ • https://medium.com/s2wblog/quick-overview-of-leaked-lockbit-3-0-black-builder-program-880ae511d085
ATT&CKT1486 T1491.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A software installer/updater writing readme.txt into many application subfolders
  • A backup or file-sync tool restoring a tree that contains readme.txt files
  • Developer checkout of a large repo full of readme/README files (mitigated by FileCreated+single-process fan-out)
  • Documentation-generation tooling emitting readme files across a project tree
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","git.exe","robocopy.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and hash dropping the notes; confirm co-occurring encrypted-file renames and a wallpaper change (Control Panel\Desktop\Wallpaper) on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, kill the process, and block SMB write to file servers/shares; preserve a note sample and the binary (watch for self_destruct). 3) Hunt: because this variant used manual PsExec spread, sweep for PsExecSvc.exe and .KEY artifacts, the fDenyTSConnections RDP change, and the same note filename on file servers to scope blast radius and confirm no data-exfil (double-extortion) staging.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName endswith ".README.txt" or FileName endswith "readme.txt" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)restore.*files.*\.(txt|hta)"
| summarize NoteFiles = dcount(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleNote = any(strcat(FolderPath, "\\", FileName)) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, FileName
| where NoteFiles >= 15   // same-named ransom note fanned across >=15 distinct dirs = mass encryption
| order by NoteFiles desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRename","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".README.txt" or TargetFileName endswith "readme.txt" or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)restore.*files.*\.(txt|hta)"
| summarize NoteFiles = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName
| where NoteFiles >= 15   // >=15 distinct ransom-note files dropped by one process
| order by NoteFiles desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*.README.txt OR *.readme.txt OR *README.txt OR *RESTORE-MY-FILES*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/(\.README\.txt|readme\.txt|restore.*files.*\.(txt|hta))$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true))
| _count >= 15

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")

| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Watering-hole/phishing page load to DarkSword iOS credential-harvesting decoys · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to DarkSword/GHOSTBLADE iOS campaign C2 & panel infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Egress to DarkSword/GHOSTBLADE iOS campaign C2 & panel infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any managed device (including MDE-enrolled iOS) making an outbound connection to the 13 attacker IPs Censys attributed to the leaked-DarkSword operator hosting the DarkSword Admin, Decode Dashboard and C2 Control Panel front-ends. Because the harvested keychain/iCloud/Wi-Fi data is exfiltrated to these exact hosts and operators log in there to pull it, any connection is a post-exploitation GHOSTBLADE signal, not a technique template. Rationale: Pivots on the 13 IPs Censys directly attributed to the leaked-DarkSword operator (exploit panels on :8888/:3000, Decode Dashboards 103.226.155.200/201, C2 Control Panel + Apple ID decoy 103.106.190.217, tooling open-dir 93.152.221.37). Dedicated single-purpose attacker infra makes any egress high-fidelity. Corroborated against GTIG/iVerify/Lookout DarkSword research confirming the iOS 18.4-18.7 full-chain and GHOSTBLADE dataminer. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/chinese-threat-actor-uses-leaked.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/darksword-ios-exploit-chain • https://iverify.io/blog/darksword-ios-exploit-kit-explained • https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/darksword-iphone-exploit-spies-thieves
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel enrichment tooling (URLScan, Censys, VirusTotal retrohunt appliances) actively connecting to the infrastructure from a corporate egress IP
  • Malware sandbox or detonation range on the corporate network resolving/connecting to the hosts
  • A security researcher on a corporate laptop manually investigating the panels
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if one of these IPs is later re-leased to a benign tenant (re-validate IOC freshness)
  • Proxy/secure-web-gateway making a categorization fetch to the destination
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("urlscan.exe","censys.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and user; confirm the device is an iOS/iPadOS asset in the 18.4-18.7 range or any managed endpoint, and pull the full session (port, bytes, RemoteUrl) to distinguish a beacon/exfil from a one-off. 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at the firewall/SWG, isolate the device from the network, and for iOS force an OS update to a patched build and rotate the user's Apple ID, iCloud and any Wi-Fi/keychain credentials the GHOSTBLADE modules dump. 3) Hunt: sweep proxy/firewall history for any other internal host that touched these IPs, look for the Apple ID/AWS phishing-page referrers that preceded the connection, and pivot on the Telegram operator handle t.me/YATA0000 in web logs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("38.181.52.95","103.106.190.217","38.22.89.117","103.97.128.67","162.4.136.30","223.26.63.56","151.243.126.191","107.175.49.181","103.238.129.112","103.226.155.200","103.226.155.201","202.8.120.249","93.152.221.37")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocIPs = dynamic(["38.181.52.95","103.106.190.217","38.22.89.117","103.97.128.67","162.4.136.30","223.26.63.56","151.243.126.191","107.175.49.181","103.238.129.112","103.226.155.200","103.226.155.201","202.8.120.249","93.152.221.37"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in (iocIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Watering-hole/phishing page load to DarkSword iOS credential-harvesting decoys AIDelivery Medium
Hunts managed devices (esp. iOS Safari) making web requests to the operator's victim-facing delivery hosts — the Apple ID credential-harvesting decoy (103.106.190.217) and the exploit-panel front-ends on :8888/:3000 that also serve the DarkSword kit. This is the drive-by/iframe moment that fires the DarkSword JS chain, so it catches the intrusion at initial access before GHOSTBLADE is staged. Rationale: Uses the victim-facing subset of the Censys IOCs: the Hong Kong Apple ID decoy host 103.106.190.217, the Singapore front-end 38.181.52.95 running three exploit-panel builds, and the six additional exploit panels on :8888/:3000 that serve the leaked kit. Constraining to web/panel ports frames it as the watering-hole/iframe delivery step that triggers CVE-2025-31277/CVE-2026-20700 et al. before GHOSTBLADE staging. Corroborated by GTIG/iVerify DarkSword writeups describing Safari page-load drive-by delivery. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/chinese-threat-actor-uses-leaked.html • https://iverify.io/blog/darksword-ios-exploit-kit-explained • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/darksword-ios-exploit-kit-uses-6-flaws.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/darksword-ios-exploit-chain
ATT&CKT1189 T1566.002 T1203
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Secure web gateway or DLP proxy fetching the decoy page for URL categorization/rendering
  • Analyst or researcher on a corporate device manually reviewing the Apple ID / fake AWS sign-in page
  • Phishing-simulation or brand-monitoring service crawling the credential-harvesting hosts
  • IP re-lease: one of the front-end IPs later hosting a benign service on 443 (re-validate IOC currency before alerting)
  • Automated link-detonation/URL-sandbox appliance following an emailed lure to the decoy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("urlscan.exe") and SourceHostName !has "proxy" and SourceHostName !has "gateway"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source device and whether it is an iOS 18.4-18.7 asset; pull the request path/RemoteUrl and referrer to establish whether the user actually loaded the Apple ID/AWS decoy vs a passive scanner, and check for a follow-on connection to the C2/Decode-Dashboard IPs (UC1) within minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the device, block the delivery IPs and ports 8888/3000 at the SWG, and if load is confirmed on an iPhone, treat as compromised — update iOS to a patched build and rotate Apple ID/iCloud, keychain and Wi-Fi credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate every internal client that hit these hosts, search proxy logs for the AWS-console-impersonation and Apple ID lure domains/referrers, and correlate to any inbound phishing email or SMS delivering the link.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")

Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-03 10 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Non-Chrome process accessing Google Password Manager passkey Sync Data LevelDB store AIReconnaissance High
Hunts the Pass-ta-key 'Stage Zero' reconnaissance and Golden Pass-ta-key extraction: malware reading Chrome's proto-encoded WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records (usernames, credential IDs, encrypted passkey private keys) from the synced-passkey LevelDB. Article-specific because it pins the exact %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\Sync Data\LevelDB path being touched by any process other than Chrome/Google updater binaries. Rationale: Uses the exact article path %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\Sync Data\LevelDB and the WebauthnCredentialSpecifics store described as readable without elevation; any non-Chrome process touching this directory is high-fidelity because legitimate access is Chrome-only. Cross-checked against Unit 42 Part 2 and The Hacker News coverage which independently confirm the path and store. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive/Backblaze/Carbonite or other backup agents enumerating and copying the Chrome profile directory
  • Endpoint DLP or AV engines (e.g. Defender, CrowdStrike scanner) reading files in Chrome User Data during a full scan
  • IT roaming-profile / browser-migration tooling relocating Chrome profiles
  • IR/forensic collectors (KAPE, Magnet, velociraptor) triaging the endpoint during an investigation
  • Chrome extension native-messaging hosts or enterprise management agents that touch the profile
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","backblaze.exe","bzbui.exe","carbonite.exe","msmpeng.exe","csfalconservice.exe","kape.exe","velociraptor.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess (name, path, signer, SHA256) touching Sync Data; confirm it is not a signed Google/backup/AV binary and check its parent chain and whether it was recently downloaded. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the offending process/binary, and force a passkey/credential reset plus device-trust revocation for every account synced in that Chrome profile (assume passkey private-key material exfiltrated). 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256 across the fleet, look for the same process also touching passkey_enclave_state / wrapped_identity_private_key (UC2), and review outbound connections from that process for exfil of the copied LevelDB.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and FolderPath has @"\Sync Data\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","google_crashpad_handler.exe","elevation_service.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and TargetFilePath has @"\Sync Data\"
| where ActingProcessName !has "chrome.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "GoogleUpdate" and ActingProcessName !has "updater.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "elevation_service" and ActingProcessName !has "crashpad"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Process Accessing Google Password Manager Passkey Sync Store
id: 7f3a1e94-2c6b-4d18-9a5e-1b0c8f2d4e61
description: Detects a process other than Chrome/Google updater binaries creating or modifying files inside Chrome's synced-passkey LevelDB (Sync Data), where proto-encoded WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records and encrypted passkey private keys are stored. Aligns with Unit 42 Pass-ta-key Stage Zero reconnaissance / Golden Pass-ta-key extraction.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains|all:
      - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
      - '\Sync Data\'
  filter_google:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\GoogleUpdate.exe'
      - '\updater.exe'
      - '\elevation_service.exe'
      - '\google_crashpad_handler.exe'
      - '\software_reporter_tool.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_google
falsepositives:
  - Endpoint backup/sync agents enumerating the Chrome profile
  - DLP/AV scanners reading the Chrome User Data folder
  - IR/forensic collection tooling (KAPE)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Chrome\\User\ Data\\*Sync\ Data* OR *\\chrome\\user\ data\\*sync\ data*) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\GoogleUpdate.exe OR *\\updater.exe OR *\\elevation_service.exe OR *\\google_crashpad_handler.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\.*\\Sync Data\\/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(chrome|GoogleUpdate|updater|elevation_service|google_crashpad_handler|software_reporter_tool)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| count > 0
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*Sync Data*" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe","google_crashpad_handler.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*Sync Data*" NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe","google_crashpad_handler.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Non-Chrome tampering with Google passkey device-identity enclave state files AIInstallation High
Hunts the Silver/Pass-ta-key device-identity impersonation: malware writing, deleting or re-creating Chrome's passkey_enclave_state (which holds the hardware-bound identity key as an NCRYPT_OPAQUE_KEY_BLOB) or wrapped_identity_private_key to register an attacker-controlled user-verification key (device/add_uv_key) or reset device trust (device/forget). Article-specific because it targets those two named enclave files and the repeated delete/recreate pattern Unit 42 describes. Rationale: Targets the two named enclave artifacts (passkey_enclave_state holding the identity key as NCRYPT_OPAQUE_KEY_BLOB, and wrapped_identity_private_key) and the delete/recreate pattern Unit 42 ties to attacker UV-key registration; only Chrome should ever mutate these, making non-Chrome writes very low-FP. Confirmed via Unit 42 Part 2 and The Hacker News reporting on the same enclave-state manipulation. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
ATT&CKT1556 T1098
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome major-version upgrade re-initializing the passkey enclave via a transiently renamed installer/updater binary
  • IT support resetting or deleting a corrupted Chrome profile
  • Antivirus quarantining or remediating the enclave file after a (false) detection
  • Roaming-profile / folder-redirection sync agents relocating the profile directory
  • Security tooling snapshotting the enclave file for research/telemetry
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Google\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","csfalconservice.exe","onedrive.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the non-Chrome process mutating passkey_enclave_state / wrapped_identity_private_key, confirm it is unsigned or untrusted, and correlate with any prior read of the Sync Data LevelDB (UC1) on the same host/user. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate/quarantine the process, and immediately revoke device trust and force re-enrollment plus passkey reset for all accounts on that Google profile — assume an attacker UV key (device/add_uv_key) is now registered. 3) Hunt: enumerate Google account device lists for unrecognized authenticators/UV keys added in the window, sweep the fleet for the same binary SHA256, and check for outbound traffic to Google cloud-authenticator endpoints from the offending process rather than chrome.exe.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("passkey_enclave_state","wrapped_identity_private_key")
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileDeleted","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","elevation_service.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","google_crashpad_handler.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Events=count(), Actions=make_set(ActionType), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("passkey_enclave_state","wrapped_identity_private_key")
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileDeleted","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !has "chrome.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "GoogleUpdate" and ActingProcessName !has "updater.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "elevation_service" and ActingProcessName !has "crashpad"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize Events=count(), Actions=make_set(EventType), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Tampering with Google Passkey Device-Identity Enclave State Files
id: b2d9c4a7-6e31-45f8-8c0a-3f7e91a2d5c4
description: Detects a process other than Chrome/Google updater binaries writing, deleting or renaming Chrome's passkey_enclave_state or wrapped_identity_private_key files. These hold the hardware-bound device identity key; tampering enables Unit 42 Silver/Pass-ta-key device-identity impersonation and attacker UV-key registration (device/add_uv_key).
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/google-password-manager-attacks-could.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.t1556
  - attack.t1098
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\passkey_enclave_state'
      - '\wrapped_identity_private_key'
  filter_google:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\GoogleUpdate.exe'
      - '\updater.exe'
      - '\elevation_service.exe'
      - '\google_crashpad_handler.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_google
falsepositives:
  - Chrome channel upgrade under a renamed binary
  - IT-driven Chrome profile reset
  - AV quarantine of the enclave file
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:(11 OR 23) @TargetFilename:(*\\passkey_enclave_state OR *\\wrapped_identity_private_key) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\GoogleUpdate.exe OR *\\updater.exe OR *\\elevation_service.exe OR *\\google_crashpad_handler.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\(passkey_enclave_state|wrapped_identity_private_key)$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(chrome|GoogleUpdate|updater|elevation_service|google_crashpad_handler)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| count > 0
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="passkey_enclave_state" OR Filesystem.file_name="wrapped_identity_private_key") Filesystem.action IN ("modified","deleted","created","renamed") NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe","google_crashpad_handler.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="passkey_enclave_state" OR Filesystem.file_name="wrapped_identity_private_key") Filesystem.action IN ("modified","deleted","created","renamed") NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","updater.exe","elevation_service.exe","google_crashpad_handler.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
