title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

ApostropheCMS SSPP payload: $pullAll/__proto__ PATCH to piece-type API (CVE-2026-53609) AIExploitation High
Hunts the actual exploit request for CVE-2026-53609: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* whose body carries prototype-pollution keys ($pullAll, __proto__, publicApiProjection, constructor). This is the single most article-specific signal — the poisoning request that mutates Object.prototype.publicApiProjection. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC payload keys from the advisory ($pullAll, __proto__.publicApiProjection) scoped to the /api/v1/@apostrophecms/ PATCH path. Body-token match depends on WAF/proxy body logging — noted in required_telemetry. Fixed version 4.31.0 confirmed via GitLab Advisory DB and TheHackerWire. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-53609
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, Nuclei prototype-pollution templates) probing the CMS in an authorized pentest
  • Internal red-team validating CVE-2026-53609 patch status
  • Legitimate editor PATCH that coincidentally contains the literal string 'constructor' in free-text content
  • WAF telemetry replaying blocked-request samples into the SIEM for tuning
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei","nikto","sqlmap","Burp") and SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<authorized_scanner_ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request from WAF/proxy for the flagged SourceIP; confirm the body key is literally __proto__.publicApiProjection (or constructor/prototype) under a $pullAll operator, and note the HTTP response code (200 = poisoning likely succeeded). 2) CONTAIN: If the payload reached the app (not blocked), RESTART the affected Node.js process immediately — pollution persists process-wide until restart — and block the SourceIP at the WAF; verify ApostropheCMS is on <=4.30.0 and schedule upgrade to 4.31.0. 3) HUNT: Search for subsequent unauthenticated 200 responses on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global from any IP after the poisoning timestamp (see companion auth-bypass UC).
let lookback = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("WAF","ModSecurity","Application Gateway","Front Door") or isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection","constructor")
     or RequestContext has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
     or Message has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS auth-bypass symptom: protected piece-type endpoint 401/403 → 200 transition AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the impact of CVE-2026-53609: a source IP that previously received 401/403 on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user or /global begins receiving 200 responses, without any preceding successful login. This is the process-wide publicApiCheck() bypass observed on the wire. Rationale: Targets the advisory's confirmed observable: /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global flipping from notfound(401/403) to a valid 200 paginated response for unauthenticated callers. Login-IP exclusion asserts the 'unauthenticated' precondition the article emphasises. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An editor whose session cookie isn't reflected in access logs, appearing 'unauthenticated' while legitimately getting 200
  • publicApiProjection intentionally configured on a piece-type, so unauthenticated 200s are by-design for that endpoint
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor hitting the endpoint from an IP that also fails auth elsewhere
  • CDN edge caching a 200 response and serving it to varied client IPs
Suppression filter
| where uri_path in ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each flagged CIp, confirm the endpoint is one that requires auth by design (user/global) and that no successful /login/login exists for that IP; inspect whether publicApiProjection is legitimately set on the module. 2) CONTAIN: If bypass confirmed, restart the Node.js process to clear Object.prototype pollution and block the offending source IPs; upgrade to 4.31.0. 3) HUNT: Correlate the FirstSuccess timestamp backward ~minutes to find the originating PATCH with $pullAll/__proto__ (companion UC) and identify the editor account whose token performed the poisoning.
let lookback = 3d;
let loggedInIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login" and ScStatus == 200
    | distinct CIp;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where CsMethod =~ "GET"
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)   // never authenticated -> should never get 200
| summarize AuthFailures = countif(ScStatus in (401,403)),
            Successes = countif(ScStatus == 200),
            LastAuthFail = maxif(TimeGenerated, ScStatus in (401,403)),
            FirstSuccess = minif(TimeGenerated, ScStatus == 200)
            by CIp, CsUriStem
| where Successes > 0 and FirstSuccess > coalesce(LastAuthFail, datetime(1970-01-01))
| project CIp, CsUriStem, AuthFailures, Successes, LastAuthFail, FirstSuccess
| order by Successes desc

ApostropheCMS exploit chain: unauth PATCH to /@apostrophecms/global → 200 GET on /user within 30s AIExploitation High
Correlates the two-step CVE-2026-53609 exploit: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* from an IP that never authenticated, immediately followed (≤30s) by a successful 200 GET on a normally-protected piece-type endpoint from the same IP. Sequencing raises confidence over either event alone. Rationale: Encodes the PoC step sequence from the advisory (Step 3 PATCH poisoning -> Step 4 unauthenticated 200 on /user) as a same-source temporal join with a 30s window and a never-authenticated precondition, yielding a high-fidelity, low-FP correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanner running the exact PoC sequence during an authorized assessment
  • Editor whose auth cookie is stripped from access logs, so a legitimate PATCH+GET pair looks unauthenticated
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites method/path causing spurious PATCH-then-GET pairing
  • publicApiProjection legitimately enabled, making the trailing GET a by-design 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve both correlated requests for the CIp; confirm the PATCH body carried $pullAll/__proto__ and the GET returned a real result set rather than notfound. 2) CONTAIN: Restart the Node.js process to purge the polluted prototype, block the source IP, and rotate/disable any editor account whose token appears on the PATCH. 3) HUNT: Expand the window to enumerate every unauthenticated 200 to all piece-type endpoints after PatchTime; check for data exfiltration volume and pivot on the editor account for prior suspicious PATCH activity.
let win = 30s;
let lookback = 2d;
let loggedInIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login" and ScStatus == 200
    | distinct CIp;
let patches = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsMethod =~ "PATCH" and CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
    | where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)
    | project PatchTime = TimeGenerated, CIp, PatchUri = CsUriStem;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where CsMethod =~ "GET" and ScStatus == 200
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)
| join kind=inner patches on CIp
| where TimeGenerated between (PatchTime .. PatchTime + win)
| project PatchTime, GetTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, PatchTime), CIp, PatchUri, GetUri = CsUriStem
| order by PatchTime desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as GetTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.status=200 (Web.uri_path="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user" OR Web.uri_path="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global") by Web.src Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| join type=inner src [
    | tstats `summariesonly` max(_time) as PatchTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=PATCH Web.url="*/api/v1/@apostrophecms/*" by Web.src
    | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` ]
| where GetTime >= PatchTime AND GetTime <= (PatchTime + 30)
| eval DelaySec = GetTime - PatchTime
| convert ctime(PatchTime) ctime(GetTime)
| table src uri_path PatchTime GetTime DelaySec
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as GetTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.status=200 (Web.uri_path="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user" OR Web.uri_path="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global") by Web.src Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| join type=inner src [
    | tstats summariesonly=false max(_time) as PatchTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=PATCH Web.url="*/api/v1/@apostrophecms/*" by Web.src
    | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` ]
| where GetTime >= PatchTime AND GetTime <= (PatchTime + 30)
| eval DelaySec = GetTime - PatchTime

| table src uri_path PatchTime GetTime DelaySec
Exposed ApostropheCMS instances (CVE-2026-53609) asset-exposure hunt AIReconnaissance Low
Inventories which internet-facing hosts/sites serve ApostropheCMS piece-type REST endpoints (/@apostrophecms/), so the SOC can scope CVE-2026-53609 exposure and prioritise upgrade to 4.31.0. A discovery/hunting sweep, not an alert. Rationale: The advisory names the product family (ApostropheCMS) and vulnerable range (<=4.30.0, fixed 4.31.0). Enumerating hosts serving /@apostrophecms/ endpoints is the concrete, log-derivable way to scope exposure without inventing version banners. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-53609
ATT&CKT1592
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Every legitimate ApostropheCMS site in the estate appears — this is inventory, not malice
  • Static asset requests under /@apostrophecms/ media paths inflating counts
  • Internal staging/dev instances mixed with production hosts
  • Third-party or vendor-hosted Apostrophe sites appearing in shared proxy logs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each host/site returned, confirm it is genuinely ApostropheCMS and determine the running version (check package.json / release notes / vendor). 2) CONTAIN: For any instance <=4.30.0, prioritise upgrade to 4.31.0 and apply the __proto__/constructor/prototype path-segment rejection; restrict editor account provisioning. 3) HUNT: On confirmed-vulnerable hosts, run the payload-detection and auth-bypass UCs retroactively over 30d to check for prior exploitation.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsUriStem has "/@apostrophecms/"
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SamplePaths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20)
            by CsHost
| order by Requests desc

Atomic Arch AUR loader/stealer known-bad file & process hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or on-disk presence of the July 2026 AUR (openconnect-sso) two-stage loader and Rust infostealer by their published SHA256/MD5 hashes. Article-specific: these hashes belong to the IFIN-analyzed Atomic Arch campaign redistributed through hijacked AUR package adoptions. Rationale: Uses the four campaign SHA256 hashes plus the MD5 pre-extracted from the article; SHA256 6144d433... is independently confirmed as the Rust stealer binary by The Hacker News and GuardSix, so hash-based matching is high-fidelity with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://discourse.ifin.network/t/new-aur-attack-prompts-adoption-lock/698
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an authorized sandbox that reports to production EDR
  • Threat-intel/VirusTotal retrohunt downloads of the sample onto a research host
  • Incident-response tooling copying the artifact for evidence collection
  • Backup/AV quarantine re-scanning a previously captured copy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("clamscan","freshclam","vt","virustotal") and FolderPath !has "/quarantine/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is Arch/Arch-based and whether any AUR package (openconnect-sso, boringssl-git, icloudpd, windscribe-cli-v2-bin, stirling-pdf-desktop-bin, pgadmin4-server) was recently installed/updated via makepkg. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the matching PID, and treat all local secrets (SSH keys, browser creds, cloud/dev/AI tokens) as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, systemd units with Restart=always, and cron entries; rotate SSH keys and check known_hosts targets for lateral spread.

Tor client masquerading as dbus-daemon making external network connections AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Atomic Arch first-stage behaviour of launching a Tor client renamed to 'dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion C2. A legitimate dbus-daemon is a local IPC bus and never initiates public/internet egress, so any outbound public connection from a dbus-daemon process is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article states the loader 'downloads and launches a Tor client disguised as dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion server; corroborated by GuardSix noting C2 via a Tor onion service. dbus-daemon making public egress (Defender/Falcon) or running outside /usr/bin (Sentinel/Datadog/Sigma) is essentially never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom-built dbus deployed to a non-standard prefix (/usr/local/bin) on developer boxes — path variant only
  • D-Bus remote/TCP transport intentionally configured in a container or CI runner
  • Chaos/network-testing tooling renamed to system binaries during red-team exercises
  • Flatpak/snap sandboxes shipping their own dbus-daemon under /app or /snap paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !in~ ("/usr/bin","/usr/local/bin") or RemotePort in (9001, 9030, 9050, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full path, hash, and command line of the dbus-daemon process; a real one lives at /usr/bin/dbus-daemon and only talks to unix sockets — confirm the destination IP/port and whether it looks like a Tor guard node (443/9001). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the process; block the destination IP at egress. 3) Hunt: locate the parent AUR build (makepkg), the second-stage stealer under /var/lib or ~/.config, and any systemd/cron persistence; rotate all secrets on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dbus-daemon"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "dbus-daemon"
| where TargetProcessName !has "/usr/bin/dbus-daemon"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-package-manager process writing systemd unit or cron persistence (Atomic Arch) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the loader's persistence step: writing a systemd service (Restart=always) to /etc/systemd/system or ~/.config/systemd/user, plus cron jobs, from a process that is NOT a package manager or systemctl. Article-specific to the AUR loader installing systemd services and cron jobs after anti-analysis checks. Rationale: Article states the loader 'installs systemd services and cron jobs to ensure persistence'; StepSecurity/GuardSix confirm a Restart=always unit dropped to /etc/systemd/system (root) or ~/.config/systemd/user (user). Keying on non-package-manager writers to these exact paths captures the malicious writer while excluding legit installs to /usr/lib/systemd/system. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hand-authoring a unit with a text editor (vim/nano) or writing crontab via a script
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt) deploying systemd units or cron jobs
  • Developer enabling a user service under ~/.config/systemd/user for a legitimate app
  • Container build steps or dotfile-management tools writing unit files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","vim","nano","vi","tee") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef","salt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped unit/cron file — malicious ones point ExecStart at a binary under /var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp or /dev/shm and use Restart=always; benign ones point at packaged binaries in /usr/bin. 2) Contain: disable/remove the unit or cron entry, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host if the target is a non-package path. 3) Hunt: pivot to the writing process's ancestry (makepkg build?), check for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process and stealer artifacts, and rotate host secrets.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.config/systemd/user/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/")
| where FileName endswith ".service" or FolderPath has "cron"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","dnf","yum","install","crontab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.config/systemd/user/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/")
| where TargetFilePath endswith ".service" or TargetFilePath has "cron"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","rpm","dnf","crontab"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SSH worm: persistence-path binary spawning ssh/scp for self-propagation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Atomic Arch stealer's SSH worm capability — a binary running from a malware persistence directory (/var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp, /dev/shm) spawning ssh/scp/sftp/rsync to copy and execute itself on other hosts using stolen SSH keys. Distinguishes malware-driven lateral movement from interactive/administrative SSH. Rationale: Article states the stealer 'can spread laterally by using stolen SSH keys to copy and execute itself on other systems'; corroborated by StepSecurity/HackerNews noting SSH-key and known_hosts theft. Anchoring on ssh/scp spawned by a parent living in the confirmed persistence directories (/var/lib for root, ~/.config for user) targets the worm rather than routine admin SSH. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom deployment/orchestration scripts installed under /var/lib or a user's ~/.config wrapper that call scp/rsync
  • CI/CD runner or backup agent staged in /tmp or /var/lib performing rsync-over-ssh
  • Developer helper tools in ~/.config invoking git-over-ssh (partly excluded via git filter)
  • Config-management agents copying files to fleet hosts over ssh
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","rsnapshot","borg","restic","rclone") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitlab-runner","buildkite-agent","jenkins")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent binary's path, hash, and the ssh/scp command line — note the destination host/user and whether a copy of the parent binary is being transferred. 2) Contain: isolate the source host, kill the process, and pre-emptively isolate the destination host(s) named in the command line; revoke/rotate the SSH keys used. 3) Hunt: on each destination host, hunt for the same persistence (systemd Restart=always, cron), the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, and the campaign hashes; expand outward via known_hosts entries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git","ansible","ansible-playbook","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh","code")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/ssh","/scp","/sftp","/rsync")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("/git","/ansible","/bash","/sh","/zsh","/fish","/rsync","/ssh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: d7b3f981-2c44-4a90-9e15-3b8c6a1f2e57

detection:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency

BleepingComputer
2026-07-31 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Online advertising firm Adform suffered a supply-chain attack that delivered cryptocurrency-stealing scripts to websites using its ad platform, replacing wallet addresses copied to visitors' clipboards with ones controlled by an attacker. [...]

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the attacker-controlled server (84.32.102.230, port 7744) that the trojanized Adform scripts beaconed to, exfiltrating victim IP, referring website and URL path. Any host reaching this IP indicates a browser that loaded the compromised trackpoint-async.js during the July 2026 supply-chain window. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the attacker-controlled C2 confirmed in both Beaumont's DoublePulsar analysis and BleepingComputer; it is not owned by Adform and has no benign use, making any connection a high-fidelity indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002 T1115
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware sandbox intentionally detonating the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner/crawler validating the C2 from an internal host
  • IP later reassigned to a benign shared-hosting tenant (verify port 7744 and date window July 2026)
  • Corporate VPN/proxy egress IP coincidentally matching (unlikely - it's a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user and initiating process for the connection; confirm it is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe/firefox.exe) and whether the timestamp falls in the 26-27 July 2026 window. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at firewall/proxy, and if repeated beaconing is seen, isolate the host and force browser cache/cookie clearing per Adform's guidance. 3) Hunt: pivot to all other hosts that touched this IP, warn affected users to re-verify any crypto wallet addresses they copied/pasted recently, and check for the malicious script hash (see companion UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunts the fleet for the exact malicious trojanized Adform tracking library (SHA256 02ff86c7...) landing on disk, typically as a browser cache artifact, to scope which endpoints downloaded the crypto-clipper during the supply-chain window. VirusTotal flagged this file clean across all engines, so hash-based hunting is required rather than AV signal. Rationale: SHA256 02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55 is the pre-extracted hash of the injected library; because VirusTotal shows zero detections, an exact-hash file hunt is the only reliable way to scope endpoint exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1115 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DFIR analyst intentionally saving the sample to an endpoint for analysis
  • A copy of the sample pulled from Beaumont's Pastebin/Archive.org for internal review
  • Malware-repo or IOC-feed clone stored on a workstation
  • SHA256 collision (cryptographically negligible - treat any exact match as true positive)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path (browser cache dir vs a saved copy) and the FileOriginUrl/downloading process to distinguish a real infection from analyst handling. 2) Contain: on genuine infections, clear the affected browser's cache/cookies as Adform advises, block 84.32.102.230, and advise the user to re-check any crypto addresses copied on 26-27 July 2026. 3) Hunt: correlate matching hosts against the C2-beacon UC, and search proxy logs for retrievals of trackpoint-async.js from s2.adform.net/a1.adform.net/ai1.adform.net during the window to build the full impacted-user list.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("trackpoint-async.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("trackpoint-async.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-31 17 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, has been observed compromising the sign-in portals of hospitality-related organizations such as hotels since May 2026 in order to deliver malware to travelers and steal credentials in an operation we call CaptiveCrunch. The post CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure · [LLM] CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CornFlake RAT persistence via svchost32.exe masquerade in %APPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts Storm-2945's CornFlake implant, which copies itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and registers as a Windows service 'svchost32' (display name 'Cloud Sync Service') to masquerade as the legitimate System32 svchost.exe. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever runs from %SystemRoot%\System32, so any svchost32.exe under a user profile path is malicious by construction. Rationale: Anchored on the exact drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and service name 'svchost32'/'Cloud Sync Service' from the article; corroborated by ReliaQuest and The Hacker News. A binary named svchost32.exe outside System32 has no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party app that legitimately ships a file literally named svchost32.exe in AppData (extremely rare; none known)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the CornFlake sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • EDR sample-detonation or red-team emulation of this exact campaign
  • Backup/restore of an already-infected profile re-writing the path
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the SHA256 of svchost32.exe and confirm the parent process and the '\svchost32\svchost32.exe' path is under a user profile (never System32). Check for a service named svchost32 with display 'Cloud Sync Service'. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop and delete the svchost32 service, remove the Run key and scheduled task pointing at the binary, and force-revoke the user's Entra sessions/tokens (traveler likely token-compromised). 3) HUNT: Sweep for the same path/service org-wide, and pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from svchost32.exe and to the doppelganger M365 domains/IOC IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" or FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=NewProcessName, Detail=CommandLine, Actor=SubjectUserName),
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4697 | where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=ServiceName, Detail=ServiceFileName, Actor=SubjectUserName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections and DNS lookups to the Storm-2945 doppelganger domains that mimic Microsoft 365 services (ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com) and the campaign's actor-controlled IP infrastructure used for adversary-in-the-middle device-code phishing and M365 token theft. These are hard IOCs — any hit indicates a traveler routed through the CaptiveCrunch AiTM proxy. Rationale: Uses the article's exact doppelganger domain list and pre-extracted actor IP set (Block 2), cross-checked against ReliaQuest's write-up of the same infrastructure. These are unique lookalike domains with zero legitimate business use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security tool / TI feed pre-fetching or sinkholing these IOC domains for analysis
  • Analyst manually browsing to the domain during investigation from a corporate host
  • Passive DNS / URL-scanning services running from the monitored range
  • IP reuse after takedown where the IP is reassigned to a benign host (verify domain hit alongside IP)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify which user/device connected and whether the connection carried an M365 auth flow (browser process, Referer to login.microsoftonline.com). Confirm the device was on untrusted Wi-Fi (hotel/conference). 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's Entra refresh tokens and sign-in sessions immediately, require re-registration of MFA, and block the domains/IPs at proxy and firewall. 3) HUNT: Check Entra sign-in logs for the same user authenticating from the actor IPs and for any new device registration; sweep the endpoint for CornFlake (svchost32.exe) delivered on the same session.

| where RemoteUrl has_any(target_domains) or RemoteIP in (target_ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc

(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (target_domains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, Result)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful Entra ID authentications originating from Storm-2945's actor-controlled IP infrastructure, the tail end of the CaptiveCrunch device-code AiTM flow where a phished traveler's device code authenticates the attacker's session. Anchors on the campaign's confirmed IP set as the sign-in source. Rationale: Anchors on the article's actor IP set as the authentication source — a successful M365 sign-in from CaptiveCrunch infrastructure is a direct token-theft indicator; Volexity independently documents the same device-code AiTM technique for this actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/ • https://phishingtackle.com/blog/russian-hackers-use-microsoft-device-code-phishing-in-targeted-attacks
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528 T1098.005
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned by its hosting provider to a benign VPN/proxy a legitimate user transits
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance replaying sign-in test traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally sharing a subnet with a taken-down IOC (verify exact /32)
  • Analyst reproducing the auth flow from an actor IP in a lab tenant
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the sign-in succeeded (ErrorCode/ResultType 0) and identify the app (Graph, OWA) and whether a new device was registered in the same window. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke all refresh tokens for the account, disable the account or force password reset + MFA re-enrollment, and remove any attacker-registered device from Entra. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the account to Graph/EWS mail-access and any OAuth app consent grants; check the user's endpoint for CornFlake and correlate to the doppelganger-domain connections from UC2.

ClickFix execution reaching CaptiveCrunch infrastructure or dropping svchost32 AIDelivery High
Detects the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix chain where a user is socially engineered (fake browser/OS update) into running a script interpreter whose command line reaches Storm-2945's doppelganger domains/IOC IPs or references the CornFlake drop path svchost32. Anchors the generic ClickFix pattern to this campaign's concrete IOCs to avoid template noise. Rationale: Pairs the ClickFix execution primitive (interpreter launch) with the campaign's hard IOCs (doppelganger domains, actor IPs, svchost32 drop path) so it fires only on this campaign, not on generic scripting — combination is high-fidelity per the article's ClickFix delivery description. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Threat-hunting query copy-pasted into a console leaving IOC strings in a shell history/command line
  • Sinkhole or research tooling curling the IOC domains for analysis
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full command line — confirm which IOC it hit (domain download vs svchost32 reference) and the parent process (explorer.exe/browser indicates ClickFix paste). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any child svchost32.exe, and revoke the user's Entra tokens (traveler credential exposure). 3) HUNT: Pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the svchost32 drop and DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on C2 to the IOC IPs; sweep other travelers for the same ClickFix command shape.

CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network connections initiated by the CornFlake implant running as svchost32.exe from a user AppData path. The legitimate svchost.exe lives only in System32 and its network activity is service-mediated, so public-internet egress from a profile-resident svchost32.exe is CornFlake C2 / data exfiltration beaconing. Rationale: Anchors on the CornFlake implant image/path (svchost32.exe under AppData, from the article) making outbound public connections — behaviorally impossible for the real System32 svchost.exe, so any hit is CornFlake beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox detonation of the CornFlake sample generating C2 traffic on a monitored host
  • Red-team emulation using a binary named svchost32.exe
  • A misconfigured third-party tool coincidentally named svchost32.exe (none known)
  • EDR telemetry replay/testing environments
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm InitiatingProcessFolderPath is a user AppData path and capture the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl destinations (correlate to the campaign IOC IPs). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, terminate svchost32.exe, remove its service/Run key/scheduled task persistence, and block the C2 destinations. 3) HUNT: Retrieve collected-data artifacts (keylogger/screenshot/audio files), revoke the traveler's Entra tokens, and sweep the fleet for the same process-to-public-IP pattern and the svchost32 drop path.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
